papers.title: When Elements Fail: Weighted Fault-Tolerant Matroid Bases
papers.abstract: Given a rank-\(r\) matroid on \(n\) elements with nonnegative costs and a partition into safe and vulnerable elements, we seek a minimum-cost set that spans after every deletion of at most \(k\) selected vulnerable elements. We resolve several open questions posed by Bentert, Fomin, Golovach, and Morelle (ESA 2025) concerning weighted costs, nonuniform failures, and explicitly specified failure scenarios. To this end, we develop two compression methods. For matroids given by an independence oracle, weighted flat-avoidance representatives yield a bounded subset of the ground set containing an optimal solution and a \(2^{\mathcal{O}((r+k)^4)}n^{\mathcal{O}(1)}\)-time algorithm. This establishes fixed-parameter tractability for weighted costs and nonuniform failures simultaneously. For explicitly represented linear matroids, polynomial certificates allow us to compress families of partial solutions while preserving successful completions under all allowed failures. This yields a deterministic algorithm using \(2^{\mathcal{O}(kr(r+k)\log(r+1))}n^{\mathcal{O}(1)}\) field operations over arbitrary fields. Over fixed finite fields, a simpler reduction uses parallel classes. For explicitly listed failure scenarios, we obtain fixed-parameter algorithms parameterized by rank and the number of scenarios. In contrast, the size-budget decision version is W[1]-hard parameterized by rank and maximum scenario size, even on uniform matroids with two-element scenarios. \keywords{Matroids \and Fault tolerance \and Fixed-parameter algorithms \and Representative families}

papers.title: Individually Fair Facility Location
papers.abstract: We study individually fair facility location, where each client must connect to an open facility within a prescribed radius and the objective is to minimize total opening and connection cost. We show that preserving the radii changes the approximability of metric facility location fundamentally. For every fixed radius violation below three, no deterministic polynomial-time algorithm achieves a sublogarithmic cost factor unless $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}$. The hardness holds with uniform opening costs and uniform radii. It contradicts the strict-fairness constant-factor guarantee recently claimed by Liu, Xu, and Zhang [Theory of Computing Systems, Vol. 70 (2026)]. We then establish a positive result for arbitrary client radii. We give a randomized polynomial-time algorithm that has cost at most $1.725$ times the strictly fair optimum and serves every client within three times its fair radius (in the Appendix we show how this can be de-randomized). We use the approach of Byrka, Srinivasan and Swamy [IPCO 2010]. The facility-location radius factor three is therefore optimal among deterministic polynomial-time algorithms with constant cost factor, unless $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}$. Experiments on real-world data indicate that the worst case radius bound is rarely realized in practice: the algorithm serves over 99.8% of clients within their stated radius, and never beyond 1.5 times it. Our code is available at https://github.com/milindmaiti/IFFL_Implementation.

Our key observation is that we can apply forward differentiation to the backpropagation circuit, with only constant overhead over a forward sketch of the same Taylor degree. papers.title: Designing Information in a Forest: Algorithmic Aspects
papers.abstract: The Bayesian persuasion framework models strategic information revelation by a sender to one or more receivers. We study an intricate version of the multi-receiver persuasion setting in which the communication hierarchy is a forest - i.e., some receivers observe more informative signals than others, and the partial ordering of the receivers according to the information they get is represented by a pre-specified directed forest. This model naturally captures interactions in hierarchical organizations, and it lies in between the two most commonly studied versions of Bayesian persuasion: private persuasion and public persuasion. Inspired by the classic model of private persuasion, we focus on a setting with a binary state of nature and binary-action heterogeneous receivers s.t. the sender's utility is a monotone function of the set of receivers taking a specific desirable action. We extend the computational tractability result for symmetric sender's utility from private persuasion to the forest hierarchy framework using methodology inspired by optimal transport theory. We further provide a polynomial-time algorithm when the sender's utility is modular. On the negative side, we show that, unlike in private persuasion, the case of a supermodular sender's utility function leads to an NP-hard optimization problem which further does not admit an FPTAS unless P=NP; this result holds even when each tree component of the forest is a chain of 3 receivers. To complement the hardness result, we provide a simple approximation algorithm with the approximation ratio depending linearly on the depth of the forest hierarchy. We further provide an analogous algorithm for the submodular utility case. Finally, beyond forest communication hierarchies, we rule out an FPTAS for the sender's optimal utility even in the symmetric utility case, unless P=NP.

papers.title: Weak Composition Theorems for Randomized Communication

The Kneser graph $K(n,k)$ is the graph whose vertex set corresponds to the family of $k$ sized subsets of an $n$ sized ground set, and a pair of vertices are adjacent if and only if the corresponding sets are disjoint. In this short paper, we provide new bounds for the boxicity of $K(n,k)$. We first show that for $k\ge 2$ and $n\ge 2k+1$, $\operatorname{box}(K(n,k))\ge n-2k$, thereby improving the lower bounds of Caoduro and Lichev [Discrete Mathematics 346(5):113333 (2023)] when $n\geq 3k+1$ and $k\ge 3$. The proof of this result uses the topological method and follows a strategy similar to Greene's proof of the Kneser's conjecture on the chromatic number of $K(n,k)$. We also show that for $k\ge 2$, $t\ge 1$ and $n=2k+t$, $\operatorname{box}(K(2k+t,k)) \leq O( t^3\log(2k+t) ).$ In particular, for every $t=t(k)\ge1$ with $t^3\log k=o(k)$, $\operatorname{box}(K(2k+t,k))=o(k)$. This is the first upper bound on the boxicity of $K(n,k)$ that is sublinear in $n$. We also show that for large enough $k$, $\operatorname{box}(K(2k+1,k))\le \frac{3\ln (2k+1)}{\ln\ln (2k+1)}$.

papers.title: The Tournament Equilibrium Set Is PSPACE-Complete, Even under Hereditary Uniqueness
papers.abstract: The tournament equilibrium set (TEQ), proposed by Schwartz in 1990, is a classical voting rule based on pairwise majority comparisons. Its definition is recursive: an alternative is judged by the alternatives that beat it, called its dominators, and by which of those dominators TEQ itself selects. Deciding whether a given alternative belongs to TEQ was known to be NP-hard and to lie in PSPACE. We close this gap by proving that the problem is PSPACE-complete. To our knowledge, this is the first PSPACE-completeness result for membership in a tournament solution. The hardness persists even when every nonempty subtournament has a unique minimal retentive set, the property conjectured by Schwartz to hold for all tournaments. Moreover, every such subtournament in our hard instances contains an alternative with at most three dominators. We prove that a single alternative with at most four dominators suffices both to guarantee uniqueness and to find a TEQ winner in $O(N^2)$ time. Thus, on our hard instances, finding one winner is efficient even though recognizing a specified winner is PSPACE-complete. We also study how the complexity changes with the dominator bound. If every nonempty subtournament has an alternative with at most one dominator, the entire TEQ can be computed in quadratic time; allowing two dominators makes membership NP-hard. Under the same condition with four dominators, all $t$ winners can be computed in $O(2^t N^2)$ time, where $N$ is the number of alternatives.

papers.title: A Binary Search Tree with the Unified Bound
papers.abstract: We give a deterministic online binary search tree (BST) that satisfies the unified bound of Iacono [SODA 2001], which subsumes the working-set and dynamic-finger bounds: it serves every sequence $X$ of $m$ searches on $n$ keys at total cost $O(m+\mathrm{UB}(X))$, and every single search at cost $O(\log n)$. Previously, no BST was known to satisfy the unified bound, even offline. As a consequence, the dynamic optimality conjecture implies Iacono's conjecture that splay trees satisfy the unified bound. We also show that the unified bound is $O((m+n)(1+\log c_σ))$ on every sequence of searches that avoids a fixed permutation $σ$, where $c_σ$ is the Füredi-Hajnal limit of $σ$. Hence every BST that satisfies the unified bound, including ours, serves such sequences at this cost. For permutations this bound is tight, and it improves the previous upper bound $O(nc_σ^2)$ on the optimal cost, due to Berendsohn, Kozma and Opler [STOC 2024]. Finally, we extend the tree to support insertions and deletions: a sequence $X$ of $m$ operations, starting from $n_0$ keys, costs $O(n_0+m+\mathrm{UB}(X))$ in total, where $\mathrm{UB}$ is now the extension of the unified bound to insertions and deletions by Bădoiu, Cole, Demaine and Iacono [TCS 2007]. Hence, if splay trees are dynamically optimal for searches, insertions and deletions, then they serve every such sequence at this total cost as well.

papers.title: Tight Cycle-Cover Inequalities and Improved Approximation for Shortest Common Superstring with Reverse Complements
papers.abstract: The Shortest Common Superstring (SCS) problem is a classical idealized model of genome assembly. However, SCS does not account for the double-stranded nature of DNA: sequencing reads may originate from either strand without a known orientation. This motivates a natural variant, Shortest Common Superstring with Reverse Complements (SCS-RC), which asks for a shortest string containing each input string or its reverse complement as a substring. For SCS, the MGREEDY algorithm constructs an optimal cycle cover of the overlap graph and concatenates the strings obtained by breaking each cycle at its minimum-overlap edge. This algorithm was recently shown to achieve a tight $3$-approximation. Its reverse-complement extension, MGREEDY-RC, also constructs an optimal cycle cover of the overlap graph augmented with reverse complements, but its best known approximation guarantee was $3.75$ (CPM 2026). We extend this cycle-cover inequality to SCS-RC and show that MGREEDY-RC achieves a $3$-approximation, which is tight even over the DNA alphabet. The $3$-approximation guarantee for MGREEDY-RC yields a $2.5$-approximation for TGREEDY-RC, which greedily merges the strings derived from the cycle cover. By replacing this greedy merging step with an algorithm based on a reduction to a maximum-weight Hamiltonian path problem constrained to contain a given perfect matching, we obtain a $(22/9+\varepsilon)$-approximation for every fixed $\varepsilon>0$. This improves upon the previous best ratio of $8/3$ (WABI 2026), establishing the best known polynomial-time approximation guarantee for SCS-RC.

papers.title: Online Transportation via Shifted Geometric Scales
papers.abstract: In the Online Transportation problem, introduced by Kalyanasundaram and Pruhs (1995), requests arrive sequentially in a metric space and must be assigned immediately and irrevocably to one of $m$ facilities with available capacity. The objective is to minimize the total distance between requests and their assigned facilities. The problem generalizes the Online Metric Matching problem, in which each facility has unit capacity, and inherits a $2m-1$ lower bound on the competitive ratio for all deterministic algorithms. For Online Metric Matching, Kalyanasundaram and Pruhs (1993) and Khuller, Mitchell, and Vazirani (1994) established an optimal deterministic competitive ratio of $2m-1$, attained by the Retrospective (Permutation) algorithm. Kalyanasundaram and Pruhs (1998) conjectured that the same ratio is achievable for online transportation. Recently, Seth, Das, and Raghvendra (2026) obtained a competitive ratio of approximately $6.66m-2.89$ using their Robustified Greedy algorithm. We give an algorithm with competitive ratio $ρ(m-1)+1$, where $ρ\approx5.64$. Our algorithm builds on minimum-spanning-tree search techniques developed by Harada and Itoh (2025) and Arndt, Moseley, Pruhs, and Uetz (2026), using priority-based virtual depth-first searches over the known facilities. However our algorithm uses a phase to shift the geometric search scales, to decide when to skip certain searches and optimize the thresholds that define what edges to include in a given search.

papers.title: A Little Length Slack Goes a Long Way in Planar Length-Constrained Network Design
papers.abstract: Problems in length-constrained network design ask for min-cost subgraphs connecting $k$ input vertex pairs by paths of length at most $h$. Algorithms that instead connect these pairs by paths of length at most $βh$ are said to have length slack $β$. Recent work has shown that poly-time polylogarithmic approximations with polylogarithmic length slack are possible for a broad class of both directed and multicommodity length-constrained network design problems on planar graphs. We give the first poly-time polylogarithmic approximations with $O(1)$ length slack for these problems on planar graphs. In particular, for the length-constrained setting, we give LP-competitive algorithms for planar graphs with length slack $1+ε$ and approximation ratios of $O(\log^2 k/ε)$ for directed Steiner tree and $O(\log^5 k/ε^2)$ for (undirected) Steiner forest. Similarly, for length-constrained directed Steiner forest, we give an $O(\log^6 k/ε)$ approximation on planar graphs with length slack $6+ε$. Our approach is based on a novel charging argument that charges the cost of our solution to the length of the LP and the length of our solution to the cost of the LP. We complement these algorithms with hardness results that separate planar and general graphs for both forest problems: under standard complexity assumptions, we rule out polylogarithmic approximations on general graphs with length slack below $3$.

papers.title: A One-Sided Sublinear-Query Tester for Bounded-Degree 2SAT
papers.abstract: We give a one-sided tester for satisfiability of 2CNF formulas in the bounded-degree model. For every degree bound $Δ$, distance parameter $\varepsilon>0$, and $ν\in(0,1/2)$, its query complexity on $n$-variable formulas is $\widetilde O_{\varepsilon,Δ,ν}(n^{1/2+ν})$.

papers.title: Separations Between Submodular-Like Graph Widths
papers.abstract: Many algorithmic frameworks exist for evaluating join queries. They range from simple ones, such as dynamic programming over a single tree decomposition, high-degree-low-degree splitting from graph algorithms, and the degree uniformization of Joglekar and Ré, to sophisticated ones based on information-theoretic inequalities, such as the PANDA framework for submodular width. Each of these frameworks except high-degree-low-degree splitting comes with a width notion of the query that determines its running-time exponent. We fill this gap by formalizing high-degree-low-degree splitting with $\ell$ degree classes, which gives rise to the degree-splitting width $\mathrm{ds}_\ell$-width. These width notions form a hierarchy, but it was not known whether the more complicated frameworks achieve better worst-case exponents than the simpler ones on any graph query. We study this question for full self-join-free join queries with binary relations, which amounts to colored subgraph isomorphism for a pattern graph $H$. We show that every inequality in the hierarchy $\mathrm{subw} \le \#\mathrm{subw} \le \text{m-width} \le \mathrm{ds}_\ell\text{-width}$ can be strict. For instance, $\text{m-width}(K_{3,3}) = 2 < \mathrm{ds}_\ell\text{-width}(K_{3,3})$ for every constant $\ell$, so no constant number of degree classes reaches the exponent of degree uniformization. We find the smallest separating patterns, with 8, 9, and 6 nodes, respectively, by an exhaustive search with a software tool that computes these widths via mixed integer linear programming. Along the way, we give a degree-based algorithm that removes the polylogarithmic overhead of degree uniformization when evaluating full join queries. Furthermore, we show that with logarithmically many degree classes, the degree-splitting width coincides with the m-width of Joglekar and Ré. Finally, we discuss several open problems.

papers.title: Dynamic $k$-Median with Worst-Case Update Time and Recourse
papers.abstract: We study fully dynamic metric $k$-median under unit-weight client insertions and deletions. After each update, the algorithm must maintain at most $k$ centers chosen from the current client locations. We give a randomized constant-factor approximation algorithm with $\widetilde O(k)$ worst-case update time and $O((1+\logΔ)^3)$ worst-case center recourse, where $Δ$ is the aspect ratio of the underlying metric space. The approximation guarantee holds simultaneously over any prescribed finite adaptive update sequence with high probability, while the update time and recourse bounds hold on every execution. We also obtain the same asymptotic guarantees for metric $k$-means.

papers.title: An upper bound on the number of edges of a Gomory corner polyhedron
papers.abstract: We establish the first nontrivial upper bound on the number of edges of a Gomory corner polyhedron, resolving a long-standing open question. For an $n$-dimensional corner polyhedron associated with an integer lattice of determinant $δ$, the number of edges is at most $$ O\left(n6^n \cdot \bigl(1+\log_2(2δ)\bigr)^{2n-3}\right). $$ This improves the standard bound obtained by counting pairs of vertices, reducing the logarithmic exponent from $(2n-2)$ to $(2n-3)$.

papers.title: Linear Regression with Self-Selection Bias in Polynomial Time
papers.abstract: We revisit the problem of estimating $k$ linear regressors with self-selection bias in $n$ dimensions up to error $\varepsilon$ with the maximum self-selection criterion, as introduced by Cherapanamjeri, Daskalakis, Ilyas, and Zampetakis [CDIZ23, STOC]. Our main result is a $\mathrm{poly}(n,k,1/\varepsilon)$ time algorithm for the unknown-index variant of this problem, thereby improving upon the running times of the best known algorithms due to Gaitonde and Mossel [GM24] and Kalavasis, Mehrotra, and Zhou [KMZ26, COLT] with exponential dependence on $k$. Our algorithm succeeds in the presence of correlated noise between regressors, which captures the related setting of max-affine regression. Consequently, we also give the first polynomial-time algorithm for this problem, improving on the prior works of Ghosh, Pananjady, Guntuboyina, and Ramchandran [GPGR22, IEEE Transactions on Information Theory] and Gaitonde and Mossel [GM24] with exponential dependence on $k$. Prior works exhaustively search over a $k$-dimensional subspace spanned by the regressors, using conditional moments of the response to test candidates. In contrast, our algorithm is driven by an improved understanding of the moments of the covariates. We show that, restricting to observations with large response values, the degree-$(\log n)$ Hermite moment of the covariates approximately decomposes as a sum of tensor powers of the regressors. The first step of our algorithm can be viewed as a tensor decomposition algorithm for these implicitly represented high-order tensors, which outputs unit vectors parallel to the regressors. A secondary step based on a simple variant of ordinary least squares extracts estimates for the regressors given these unit vectors. We believe our analytic insight and algorithmic components may have applications to designing efficient algorithms for other latent-variable problems.

papers.title: Exact Quantum Algorithms for Composed Boolean Functions
papers.abstract: We study exact quantum algorithms for block compositions of total Boolean functions. For an outer function $f$ of degree $D$ and an inner function $g$ on $m$ bits, we prove $$ Q_E(f\circ g)=O\!\left(mD+Q_E(f)Q_{1/(4D)}(g)\right). $$ The algorithm combines approximate inner evaluations with a finite exact correction. Its two costs are governed by different parameters of the outer function: exact query complexity determines the cost of simulation, whereas polynomial degree determines the number of inner blocks used in the correction. We first establish the construction with an arity-dependent error threshold and then obtain the degree-dependent threshold above. For recursive ternary not-all-equal, this gives an exact algorithm using $(3/\sqrt2)^{k(1+o(1))}$ queries asymptotically. More generally, for every fixed nonconstant total gadget $h$, we determine the exact recursive rate as $\max\{\textrm{deg}(h),\operatorname{Adv}^{\pm}(h)\}$ and prove $Q_E(h^{\circ k})=\widetilde O_h(R(h^{\circ k})^2)$. The composition limit also allows to transfer separations from $Q_{\varepsilon}$ and $°$ to exact quantum query complexity $Q_E$ (similar to fractional block sensitivity to block sensitivity transfer in Tal and Kulkarni 2016, Chicago Journal of Theoretical Computer Science). We construct a family with $s=\operatorname{bs}=\operatorname{fbs}\ge Q_E^{3/2-o(1)}$, improving the previous exponent $1.1527\ldots$. A second construction gives $R \ge Q_E^{2-o(1)}$, improving the previous exponent $3/2$. We also allow different inner functions and give analogous quantitative separations in quantum communication.

papers.title: Core nonemptiness for $2/3$-convex games
papers.abstract: We study the core of $2/3$-convex games, a class of transferable-utility (TU) games that generalizes convex games, which requires at least two of any three distinct coalitions satisfy the supermodular inequality. We show that every $2/3$-convex game admits a marginal worth vector in the core, and hence has a nonempty core. Our proof is constructive and yields a linear-time algorithm for finding such a core allocation. We also show that $2/3$-convexity does not imply permutational convexity in general, while the implication holds under an additional superadditivity condition on pairs of singletons. As an application, we introduce a TU model motivated by the OSCE's consensus-minus-two procedure and show that the resulting game is $2/3$-convex but need not be convex.

papers.title: A Polynomial-Time Sixth-Power Excluded Grid Theorem
papers.abstract: We give a polynomial-time construction for a sixth-power excluded-grid theorem. Every graph whose treewidth is at least $g^6$ times a fixed polylogarithmic factor contains a $g\times g$ grid minor that our randomized algorithm finds with constant probability. The algorithm outputs an explicit minor model, and the exponent in its running time is independent of $g$. This improves the ninth-power existence bound of Chuzhoy and Tan~\cite{CT21} and the $g^{98}$ threshold in the polynomial-time construction of Chekuri and Chuzhoy~\cite{CC16}. Quantitative bounds relating treewidth to grid size are central to bidimensionality, developed by Demaine, Hajiaghayi, and collaborators~\cite{DH05,DH08}. The main ingredient is an asymmetric local routing theorem that uses substantially fewer attachment paths than backbone paths. A balanced recursion preserves connectivity by charging deletions to the boundary of a fixed reference cluster. We construct the smaller attachment sets through a routing hierarchy: either it exposes an accessible well-linked boundary, or its quotient graphs contain the desired grid. These arguments implement cluster splitting using approximate cuts and flow computations. An explicit cut-matching construction and a constructive grid-extraction procedure complete the algorithm. We also give a general packing--covering hypothesis for trees meeting three prescribed terminal sets under which the exponent can be reduced below six. A companion Lean development verifies the new construction, its success guarantee, and the composition of its polynomial running time, using explicit interfaces for the published algorithms and standard finite-data operations.

papers.title: Faster Deterministic All-Pairs Shortest Paths with Real Edge Weights
papers.abstract: For directed $n$-vertex graphs with arbitrary finite real edge weights and no negative cycles, we compute all-pairs distances deterministically in $O(n^{2.9929729})$ worst-case time using Uznański's half-width matrix multiplication bound. Using only the Le Gall--Urrutia rectangular multiplication bounds, our algorithm runs in $O(n^{2.99306273})$ time. This improves both the deterministic bound of $O(n^{2.9997})$ due to Chan, Itakura, Ma and Yu and the Las Vegas expected-time bound of $O(n^{2.993805})$ reported in the shreshth-s working note.

papers.title: How to Defeat a Mafia (of Size 1)
papers.abstract: The game "Mafia'' is a social deduction game where $n$ players attempt to uncover a covert coalition of $m$ players among the $n$. Typically, $d=1$ of the non-coalition players are labelled ``Detective'' and have special abilities. Most game-theoretic analysis considers, however, only the variant without a Detective. Once the Detective role is introduced, extremely complex strategies can be employed, for which reason only upper and lower bounds for winning have been established, namely by considering specific strategies. We analyse the case $m=d=1$, providing a first example where an explicit, provably-optimal strategy can be described beyond $d=0$.

papers.title: Hardness, Approximation, and Parameterized Algorithms for Asynchronous Border Minimization
papers.abstract: In the Asynchronous Border Minimization Problem (BMP), a set of DNA probe strings is placed on a grid and synthesized using a common sequence of nucleotide-deposition steps. At each step, every cell may accept or skip the offered nucleotide. The cost is the total number of disagreements between neighboring cells over all steps. We study both free placement, where the probes may be rearranged, and fixed placement, where their positions are given. We show that free-placement BMP on a square grid is NP-complete over three symbols. For one-dimensional BMP, we prove APX-hardness over a binary alphabet, and NP-completeness even when every probe has length two. We also obtain an $8/7$-approximation for the latter restriction. For square grids, we give a randomized $O(n^{1/4}\log n)$-approximation, improving the earlier $O(n^{1/4}\log^2 n)$ guarantee. Both free- and fixed-placement BMP on rectangular grids are fixed-parameter tractable when parameterized only by the allowed border cost.

papers.title: Accuracy Is Not Welfare: Evaluating AI Buyers under Strategic Price Complexity in a Synthetic Duopoly
papers.abstract: AI buying agents may alter sellers' incentives as well as consumers' decisions. In a synthetic duopoly, we evaluate price-comparison pipelines on a fixed menu and in empirical correlated-equilibrium games. Calculator assistance selects an optimal offer 84.00% of the time, versus 68.57% under verified-total disclosure, yet disclosure has a 20.14-unit higher consumer-worst equilibrium surplus. A frozen-strategy holdout comparison favors disclosure, while re-solving equilibria under scenario resampling produces a range spanning zero. These model-based results show why accuracy, loss severity, seller incentives, and welfare incidence require separate measurement.

papers.title: Sowing the Seeds of Intractability: Kalah is PSPACE-complete
papers.abstract: Kalah is a classic two-player game in the mancala family of sowing games. Computers have solved several standard-size starting positions, but the complexity of the game on boards of growing size has remained open. We study the natural generalization in which the number of pits per side is part of the input and an arbitrary position is given, with the stone counts given in unary. We show that deciding whether a designated player can force a win from such a position is PSPACE-complete. The hard positions have Alice to move first and both stores initially empty. The same positions are hard under either common convention for capture opposite an empty pit, and with or without the bonus rule, which gives a player another turn when the last stone is sown into their own store. We introduce Line Kalah as an intermediate problem, a game on a line in which stones that leave the line effectively disappear and Alice must save each of her target pits before Bob captures it, and we reduce quantified Boolean formulas to it. The reduction uses a set of sequential timer piles whose last stones approach a group of targets, forcing Alice to choose between two captures in order to set the truth value of a variable, and a final capture gadget to test a clause chosen by Bob (only one is needed adversarially). Since either player may move any pile at any time, the stages are placed so that premature timer firings protect earlier potential targets. For a true formula, Alice's strategy against arbitrary opposing play either gains enough time to save the remaining targets (after Bob deviates from the intended play) or reaches the final test with a correctly encoded, protected input. Finally, the line positions are embedded in Kalah with both stores empty. A separate Bob pit holds the score adjustment, so the winner takes a strict majority of the stones.

papers.title: Large diameter for $(Δ+2)$-colouring reconfiguration
papers.abstract: Given a graph $G$ and an integer $k$, the reconfiguration graph $\mathcal{R}_{k}(G)$ has the proper $k$-colourings of $G$ for vertices, two of which are adjacent if and only if they differ on precisely one vertex of $G$. In $2022$, Cambie, Cranston and the author proved that the diameter of $\mathcal{R}_{Δ+2}(G)$ is at most $n+2μ$, and put forth a collection of conjectures that in its strongest and most beautiful form would imply that the diameter of $\mathcal{R}_{Δ+2}(G)$ is precisely equal to $n + μ$, for every graph $G$ with $n$ vertices, matching number $μ$ and maximum degree $Δ$. Here we disprove most of those conjectures. Our constructions have reconfiguration diameter at least $n+\frac{3}{2}μ-2$. We also provide counterexamples that are $Δ$-regular, we show that every graph has reconfiguration diameter at least $n+\frac{1}{2} μ$, and we advertise an extension to hypergraphs. It is now much more mysterious how the diameter behaves, so we propose a number of open problems.

papers.title: Computation with Backward Feedback: Power, Observation, and Cost
papers.abstract: How much can a computation gain by passing information back to an earlier stage, and how soon can an observer obtain the answer? We study deterministic programs whose runs are accessed at randomly selected stages. A program keeps a register, a finite block of memory. A random clock selects the current stage; each tick takes a random step, with a law fixed independently of input, program and register. When the clock moves backward, the register contents at the stage it leaves start a new run, and the clock continues where it lands. Equilibrium readout requires a distribution of clock position and register that one tick leaves unchanged, and a correct final answer under every such distribution. For bounded steps in both directions with negative average, we obtain an exact classification at each polynomial scale s. If running time and register length are both O(s), feedback gives exactly nondeterministic space O(s); without transmission the class is deterministic time O(s), which is strictly smaller. An observer that starts at stage zero with an all-zero register, reads sequentially and never accepts a nonmember sees, with fewer ticks than any exponential, only languages fixed by a bounded input prefix. Exponentially many ticks reveal every linear-time language. For a clock moving one step up or down, we bound the wait for useful backward moves and the rate of random erasures a stored counter tolerates. The results separate the power of feedback at equilibrium, observation from a fixed start, and the cost of obtaining and keeping information.

papers.title: Exact and Approximation Algorithms for Computing Smallest SESs and BMSs
papers.abstract: Compression schemes represent repetitive strings compactly by using repeated substrings. Computing the minimum size of a representation of a given input string is important for compression and for understanding relationships between compression schemes, although this task is NP-hard for several schemes. In this paper, we introduce exact and approximation algorithms for finding smallest substring equation systems (SESs) and bidirectional macro schemes (BMSs). Specifically, for an input string of length $n$, we give deterministic and randomized algorithms for computing a smallest SES using $O^*(4^n)$ and $O^*(2^n)$ time and space, respectively. We also give a deterministic algorithm for computing a smallest BMS using $O^*(2^n)$ time and space. We further give deterministic and randomized $(1+α)$-approximation algorithms for smallest SESs using $O^*(4^{e^{-α}n})$ and $O^*(2^{e^{-α}n})$ time and space, respectively, for every $α\ge 0$. A conversion from SESs to BMSs gives $4(1+α)$-approximation algorithms for smallest BMSs with the same time and space bounds. All time bounds hold in the worst case, and the randomized algorithms return correct answers with high probability. Our algorithms adapt several approaches to exact and approximation algorithms for combinatorial problems, such as dynamic programming over determinant expansions and a greedy algorithm for monotone submodular functions.

papers.title: Fictitious Play When Agents Are Not Expected-Utility Maximizers: A Geometric Analysis in $2$-Action Games
papers.abstract: Fictitious play (FP) is one of the earliest and most fundamental learning procedures in games, where each agent independently chooses a best response to the empirical distribution of opponents' past actions by maximizing the expected payoff with respect to it. However, learning agents may not always be expected-utility maximizers: they may use nonlinear evaluation functionals to account for the uncertainty induced by the opponents, e.g., via risk measures. In this work, we study nonlinear fictitious play (NL-FP), in which each pure action is evaluated by a general, possibly nonlinear functional of the payoff distribution induced by the opponent's empirical belief. To analyze NL-FP, we first identify a single-crossing property (SCP) of evaluation functionals that preserves the classical geometry of FP in $2\times2$ games. Furthermore, we conduct a novel geometric analysis of the convergence behavior of NL-FP in $2\times2$ games, even when the SCP fails. Beyond $2\times2$ games, we show that the convergence of NL-FP in $2\times n$ ($n\ge3$) games may fail even for continuous-time NL-FP, when the two-action player uses conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) in a $2\times3$ game. In addition, we identify a finite-crossing condition that ensures convergence of the selected continuous-time dynamics and the discrete-time iterates in general $2\times n$ games, which also provides new insights into the global landscape of continuous-time classical FP in such games.

papers.title: Improved Deterministic Algorithms for $k$-SAT: Generalization of Chains and Recurrence Proof
papers.abstract: We present a deterministic algorithm for 3-SAT running in $1.32736^n$ time. The algorithm is built on a branching-and-chain framework augmented with a polynomial-time expansion procedure that joins short chains through additional clauses to form bounded-size blocks, which impose stronger constraints on the assignment space. After branching, the algorithm chooses between derandomized local search guided by the block structure and enumeration of block assignments together with selected port variables, reducing the remaining formula to 2-SAT. A weighted analysis of branching, partial-assignment, and local-search costs, together with inductive bounds for chains and block interactions, establishes the running-time guarantee. The framework is self-contained and also offers guidance for practical SAT solver design by identifying useful clause-overlap structures and suggesting when to switch between local-search and reduction-based strategies.

papers.title: Learning Dynamics of the Influencer's Game in Resource Landscapes
papers.abstract: Across domains as varied as ecology, economics, and online platforms, individuals are incentivized to position themselves within resource-rich strategy spaces. In this work we introduce a new spatial game framework called the influencer's game. Within this new framework players' strategies are represented as positions within a trait space. Players then receive a share of a portion of a resource based on their relative influence at that resource's points traits. For the influencer's game, we show that there is a unique symmetric Nash equilibrium that exists under strict log-concavity of the influence kernel. Using the unique equilibrium we show that the stability of the system depends on the influence kernel's parameters, number of players, and the resource distribution shape. For any dimension we demonstrate a stability threshold that depends on both the scatter and curvature of the players. When this threshold is crossed, the symmetric equilibrium destabilizes and gives way to a variety of bifurcation types; including, specialist clusters, limit cycles, and sub-games that reproduce the larger game's structure. We ground these results using real-world data for resources as a demonstration of the game's application. Finally we extend the game dynamics to use multi-agent reinforcement learning and further show that the predicted bifurcation structure persists under partial observability and discretized strategy spaces. In all, the influencer's game provides a novel framework for predicting when competitive pressure drives convergence versus fragmentation with possible applications across domains.

papers.title: Topological Entropy of Group Cellular Automata is Effectively Computable
papers.abstract: Topological entropy is a fundamental invariant of dynamical systems, quantifying their complexity. For cellular automata, however, determining topological entropy is generally algorithmically intractable. We study group cellular automata, namely cellular automata over a finite group alphabet whose global map is a group endomorphism. In dimension one, we decompose topological entropy into two one-sided components describing information propagating from the left and from the right in space--time. We introduce finite families of left and right traces and prove that the entropy is the sum of their growth rates. Hence, the entropy is completely determined by the growth rate of a fixed-width family of space--time patterns. This reduction from arbitrarily large windows to uniformly bounded width yields an effective procedure for computing the entropy. In particular, the entropy of every one-dimensional group cellular automaton is the logarithm of a positive integer. Using Pontryagin duality and the Bridge Theorem between topological and algebraic entropy, we also derive an explicit formula for linear cellular automata over $(\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^n$ in terms of their characteristic polynomial. Moreover, in every dimension $D\geq 2$, a group cellular automaton is either equicontinuous with zero entropy or sensitive to initial conditions with infinite entropy. Combined with decidability of equicontinuity, this implies that topological entropy is effectively computable from the local rule in every dimension. Thus, group cellular automata form a natural nontrivial class in which algebraic structure restores computability of topological entropy.

papers.title: Improved Lower Bounds for Mutually Orthogonal Latin Squares (MOLS) at 33 Orders
papers.abstract: A Latin square of order $n$ is an $n\times n$ array over symbols $\{0,1,\ldots n-1\}$, such that the same symbol does not appear twice in any row or any column. Two Latin squares of order $n$ are orthogonal if, when superimposed, they yield each of the $n^2$ ordered pairs of symbols exactly once. A set of two or more Latin squares are mutually orthogonal Latin squares (MOLS) if each pair of distinct squares is orthogonal. Let $N(n)$ be the maximum size of a set of MOLS of order $n$. For most $n$ which are not prime powers, there is a wide gap between known upper and lower bounds on $N(n)$. This has led to interest in constructing new larger sets of MOLS for explicit values of $n$, to incrementally improve the lower bounds on $N(n)$. This paper provides MOLS that improve the lower bound on $N(n)$ for 33 values of $n$ in the range from 22 through 494. The constructions were found by GPT-6 Astra, and use established techniques including difference matrices, quasi-difference matrices, orthogonal arrays, and projective planes. A highlight is 4 MOLS of order $n=22$; combined with pre-existing results, this establishes $N(n) \geq 4$ for all $n>10$.

papers.title: Asymptotic Dimension of Persistence Modules of Bounded Presentation
papers.abstract: We compute the asymptotic dimension of spaces of multiparameter persistence modules of bounded presentation under the interleaving distance. The $d$-parameter modules with at most $n$ generators and $m$ relations have asymptotic dimension, and Assouad-Nagata dimension, exactly $d(n+m)$, the number of coordinates of their generator and relation grades, over every field; for two parameters this is $2(n+m)$. The space has continuous moduli, already for two parameters and $n,m\ge2$: over an infinite field it contains, at every scale, infinite uniformly separated families of pairwise non-isomorphic modules with one fibered barcode, so it is not doubling even at a fixed fibered barcode; already for $m\ge1$ it is not coarsely equivalent to a proper metric space. The proof is an induction on the number of distinct grade coordinates: an interleaving small compared with the gaps between these coordinates moves each of them by at most twice its size and preserves the induced grid representation, so the continuous moduli are invisible at large scale. Each class of modules at finite distance therefore embeds coarsely into Hilbert space; for $n,m\ge2$ over an uncountable field, the classes that contain these families admit no such embedding into a separable Hilbert space. Under the two-parameter matching distance $2(n+m)$ is a lower bound, attained for one generator and for two generators with at most one relation; on a finite net of $S$ slices the asymptotic dimension is at most $2nS$.

papers.title: Edge-wise Graph Alignments
papers.abstract: Pairwise graph ``alignments'', usually defined as maximum common subgraphs, have been considered in many application domains, including the comparison of molecular structures. Most commonly, the problem is formulated as maximum common induced subgraph (MCIS) or maximum common edge subgraph (MCES) problems. Sometimes these formulations are restricted to connected common subgraphs. Common subgraph problems readily generalize to more than two input graphs. However, this concept is fundamentally distinct from the notion of multiple sequence alignments. Abstractly, alignments are defined as super-structures from which the individual input objects are recovered via structure-preserving projections. While the mathematical construction readily applies to common induced subgraphs, it does not fully encompass the common edge subgraph problem, which is the variant more commonly employed in cheminformatics applications. In order to consistently define multiple edge-based alignments of graphs we represent a graph $G$ as E-graph $(E,\mathscr{V})$, where $E$ is the edge set of $G$ and $\mathscr{V}$ is the set of sets of incident edges. This representation implicitly encodes the vertices in terms of edge data. Alignments of E-graphs are themselves E-graphs that contain the input (E-)graphs as subgraphs. Maximum edge subgraphs correspond to maximum induced sub-E-graphs, and they can thus be computed using a slightly modified version of the VF2 algorithm without the need to switch from graphs to line graphs. Furthermore, multiple alignments of (E-)graphs yield a natural definition of a consensus graph that is ``on average'' present in the input without having to be a subgraph of every (and in fact of any) input graph.

papers.title: Sheaf-Inspired Structured Scoring Extensions of LightGCN for Collaborative Filtering
papers.abstract: Graph-based collaborative filtering learns user and item representations by propagating embeddings over a user--item interaction graph. We investigate a modular, sheaf-inspired scoring extension placed on top of a three-layer LightGCN backbone. The motivation comes from cellular sheaves, where local vector spaces are related by linear restriction maps; here, this idea motivates structured, pair-dependent transformations of user and item embeddings rather than a change to graph propagation. We compare the identity inner-product scorer, diagonal, rank-one low-rank, and full matrix residual scorers, and a parameter-matched residual MLP baseline (\texttt{mlp\_full}) on Amazon-Book, Gowalla, MovieLens-1M, and Yelp2018. We report ranking quality and catalog coverage at cutoffs 10 and 20. The selected structured variants show modest, dataset-dependent changes in ranking quality and sometimes substantial changes in coverage. Our method is inspired by sheaf geometry but does not construct a cellular sheaf or implement sheaf-Laplacian diffusion; the experiments therefore do not establish a causal benefit from sheaf geometry itself.

papers.title: Verifiable Settlement and Pricing for Local Energy Markets: Architecture and Deployment on Hyperledger Besu
papers.abstract: We implement privacy-preserving local electricity exchanges using an automated market maker on the Hyperledger Besu network under QBFT consensus. The proposed protocol operator collects individual electricity positions off-chain and publishes aggregate supply and demand on the blockchain, where smart contracts compute market prices every fifteen minutes. Individual positions remain off-chain; Poseidon2 commitments and UltraHonk zeroknowledge proofs, generated from Noir circuits, verify aggregation, payments, and daily balance updates. The architecture retains community coordination while making financial execution independently auditable. Signed receipts and member-triggered recourse prevent unverified or partial settlement. In a ten-household experiment using simulated US residential profiles, daily settlement uses approximately 19 million gas and produces eight-member proofs in 2.4 seconds. Over four simulated days, local trading covers 34.4% of demand and reduces grid-only costs by 30.5% under assumed tariffs. Numerically computed __-Nash Equilibrium electricity profiles capture 83-88% of the social planner surplus.

papers.title: Explicit Edit Codes via Multicoloring
papers.abstract: For any fixed integers $q\ge2$ and $t\ge1$, we construct explicit $q$-ary codes of length $n$ that correct any combination of at most $t$ insertions, deletions, and substitutions, with redundancy at most $2t\log_q n+O_{q,t}(\log\log n)$ $q$-ary symbols. This matches the leading redundancy term of Levenshtein's classical existential bound. Building on the standard graph-coloring approach, we use a prime-based multicoloring of the edit-confusion graph to assign multiple colors to each $q$-ary word of length $m<n$. Appending a short, edit-protected representation of an assigned color to the length-$m$ word yields a length-$n$ codeword. The choice among the assigned colors carries additional message information, thereby reducing the redundancy. The construction admits deterministic encoding and decoding in $\widetilde O_{q,t}(n^{6t+2})$ and $\widetilde O_{q,t}(n^{7t+2})$ time, respectively.

papers.title: Regime-Uncertain Data Transactions: A Game-Theoretic Framework for Self-Adapting and Self-Diagnosing Multi-ML-Agent Systems
papers.abstract: Autonomous ML agents in large organizations exchange data and model outputs across organizational and legal boundaries. Which rules bind a given exchange is not fixed. It depends on where the data subjects live, where the agents run, who owns them, whom they target, and which version of each rule is in force. Tags that describe the data can be noisy, and a counterparty can overclaim its safeguards. We model one exchange as a \emph{regime-uncertain transfer game} between two ML agents, with an enforcer as a third player. Rules enter as hard constraints with a strictest-wins structure. Agents hold a Bayesian belief over which rules apply, can pay to unlock safeguards or verify claims, and then bargain over the remaining legal bundles.Our method, Legally-Constrained Nash Bargaining (\LCNB), implements this with a Monotonic Concession Protocol using Zeuthen's rule. We prove four properties of the model and test it in a synthetic simulator with GDPR, DPDP, CCPA/CPRA and a stylised stricter regime. In two of three stress cases where residence and citizenship differ, a citizenship-based rule violates in 21--37\% of shared records, and \LCNB{} in under 1\%. The results also show limits. With our default economics, \LCNB{} shares almost only aggregates, and its low violation rate follows partly from that. Violation tolerance, tag noise and enforcement strength matter more than the choice of bargaining solution.

papers.title: Strategically Robust Multi-Agent Control
papers.abstract: A key source of uncertainty in multi-agent systems is the behavior of other agents. Game-theoretic control approaches ignore this uncertainty, while robust control approaches treat others as fully adversarial. In this paper, we introduce strategically robust multi-agent control to populate the spectrum between these two paradigms. Specifically, in dynamic games, we propose that players are strategically robust and seek protection against misspecified control policies of the other players. This formulation induces a novel equilibrium concept, strategically robust dynamic equilibrium, that interpolates between game-theoretic control and robust control. We study this concept across canonical open- and closed-loop settings and show that accounting for strategic robustness also has computational benefits over classic approaches in game-theoretic control. Numerical experiments on vehicle platooning, inventory management, and network control illustrate resilience to misspecification, and also exhibit a "free-lunch" phenomenon in which strategic robustness can improve performance or social welfare.

papers.title: Triameter, distance packings, and vertex connectivity
papers.abstract: We study upper bounds for the triameter of a connected graph in terms of distance packings and vertex connectivity. For any positive integer $k$, we bound the triameter of a graph by a linear function of its $k$-packing number and show that this bound is tight for all values of the parameters. As a corollary, we confirm the conjecture of Das and Abdioğlu on the upper bound for the triameter in terms of the order and the minimum degree of a graph. We also find the maximum triameter among graphs with given order and vertex connectivity, and describe the extremal graphs. Our main tool is a projection of a graph onto a spider or a unicyclic graph which preserves the distances between three prescribed vertices.

papers.title: Visibility graphs of irregularly sampled two-dimensional fields via Voronoi tessellations
papers.abstract: Visibility graphs map a time series into a network by linking two data whenever the straight line between them is not obstructed by intermediate data. Their extension to two-dimensional fields has so far been restricted to regular lattices, where visibility is checked along a finite number of lattice directions. We propose a definition for scalar data sampled at arbitrary, irregularly scattered points of the plane. Each point is assigned its Voronoi cell, so that the data become a landscape of prisms, and two points are linked when the line of sight between them clears the cells crossed by the connecting segment. This yields horizontal ($\HVGV$) and natural ($\NVGV$) Voronoi visibility graphs that reduce exactly to the classical horizontal and natural visibility graphs when the points are collinear, contain the Gabriel graph of the point set, and can be built by an exact walk through the Delaunay triangulation. For uncorrelated heights, the horizontal graph depends only on the ranks of the data, so its statistics are independent of the marginal distribution. The probability that two points see each other is $2/[(M+1)(M+2)]$, where $M$ is the number of Voronoi cells crossed, which reduces the problem to the geometry of the tessellation. For Poisson points this gives a degree distribution with a scale-free tail $P(k)\simeq(π^3/4)\,k^{-2}$ and a mean degree that grows as $(π^3/8)\ln N$, in contrast with the finite value $\langle k\rangle=4$ of one-dimensional series. Two dimensions are therefore the marginal case in which isotropic horizontal visibility ceases to be local. Numerical simulations with up to $N=1.28\times10^5$ points support these predictions.
